messages.subject: Burrowing and climbing
parts:
Hello NicheMappers,

A reasonably straightforward question this (I think!) which I haven't been able to piece together from the ecotherm() documentation. I was wondering if an animal can still be considered 'active' (i.e. act=1 or act=2 for basking and foraging, respectively) when utilising a burrow or climbing to mitigate thermal stress?

As a quick scenario; imagine a lizard placed on the surface during the middle of the day, Tb exceeding both TPref and CTMax due to the microclimate conditions at that location. If climb=1, the lizard will be allowed to ascend a tree, potentially reducing Tb to within CTMin and CTMax, escaping the hot bounary conditions a few centimeters above the ground's surface. Would the lizard in this example be considered 'foraging' once it has climbed (let's say 20cm from the ground surface), if it's Tb is then modelled to be within CTMin/CTMax (or VTMin/VTMax)? Or has the act of escaping thermal stress made the animal 'inactive' as it seeks conditions to prevent overheating? Would the same also be true in "reverse" if the animal burrows to escape thermal stress?

I'm thinking here in the context of a real animal. Would an animal be considered 'ecologically active' (i.e. active to forage/fight/mate etc.) if it must seek dense shade/climb up a tree/hide under a rock, for example? I'd argue 'no' if the heat stress is such that the animal is carrying out activities it wouldn't otherwise have done, had conditions been different. I'm therefore curious to know how NicheMapR handles setting the activity state within a model run when shade seeking, burrowing and climbing are all permitted.

Thanks in advance.
Simon

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Burrowing and climbing
parts:
Hi Simon,

Good question. I'm about to put all the source code into the package for the ectotherm model so you'll be able to delve into the Fortran and see what it's doing in cases like this. But the way it works at present is that if it can be active within its voluntary thermal limits for foraging, within the bounds of available shade and the option of climbing (if it's turned on), it will be counted as active. The idea is that it can still 'sit and wait' for prey and potentially jump down and grab prey if they are in reach (lizards will do this) or display to other individuals. But of course for some species this may in fact represent an inability to forage/socialise, so it's not a perfect solution. When the model is running with the DEB model turned on, it will assume that food can be obtained in the case of a climber that has found a temperature within its voluntary limits up high. But other than that you can of course reclassify the activity state from the model output for whatever your particular purposes are. Another approach with respect to shade is to set more stringent limits on the maximum possible shade they can select, to match the levels you think it could obtain food under.

Hope that clears things up ...

All the best,
Mike
